content: When labor induction is necessary, oxytocin is the most commonly used agent. It is administered intravenously and adjusted to achieve the desired strength and frequency of uterine contractions. However, there is ongoing debate regarding the optimal dosing regimen and its effects on maternal and fetal outcomes, including the time from induction to delivery, mode of delivery, and the risk of uterine hyperstimulation. Current protocols for labor induction include both high-dose and low-dose oxytocin regimens, which can be delivered through continuous or pulsed infusions, with either linear or non-linear dose increments. Low-dose oxytocin protocols are generally considered safer for initiating contractions, but they may prolong the time from induction to delivery, potentially increasing the risk of fetal infection and chorioamnionitis. On the other hand, high-dose protocols may expedite delivery but carry a higher risk of uterine hyperstimulation and fetal distress. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of high-dose versus low-dose oxytocin regimens for labor induction at term. High-dose oxytocin was defined as at least 100 mU administered within the first 40 minutes, with cumulative doses reaching at least 600 mU in the first two hours. Low-dose oxytocin was defined as less than 100 mU in the first 40 minutes, with cumulative doses below 600 mU in the first two hours. The review included nine trials involving 2,391 women and their infants. The studies were assessed for eligibility, data accuracy, and risk of bias. Overall, the trials were found to have a moderate to high risk of bias. The primary outcomes showed no significant differences between high-dose and low-dose oxytocin regimens in terms of vaginal delivery not achieved within 24 hours (risk ratio [RR] 0.94, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.78 to 1.14) or cesarean section rates (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.14). There were also no significant differences in serious maternal morbidity or death (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.55 to 2.82) or serious neonatal morbidity or perinatal death (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.23 to 3.12). None of the trials reported on the incidence of uterine hyperstimulation with associated fetal heart rate changes. Secondary outcomes also revealed no significant differences between the two regimens in terms of time from induction to delivery (mean difference [MD] -0.90 hours, 95% CI -2.28 to +0.49 hours), uterine rupture (RR 3.10, 95% CI 0.50 to 19.33), use of epidural analgesia (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.18), instrumental delivery (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.66), Apgar scores below seven at five minutes (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.77 to 2.01), perinatal death (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.23 to 3.12), postpartum hemorrhage (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.34), or endometritis (RR 1.35, 95% CI 0.53 to 3.43). However, when studies with a high risk of bias were excluded, there was a significant reduction in the induction-to-delivery interval with high-dose oxytocin (MD -1.94 hours, 95% CI -0.99 to -2.89 hours). High-dose oxytocin was also associated with a significant increase in uterine hyperstimulation, although the studies did not specify whether this was accompanied by fetal heart rate changes (RR 1.86, 95% CI 1.55 to 2.25). Other secondary outcomes, such as unfavorable cervical status after 12 to 24 hours, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, neonatal intensive care unit admission, neonatal encephalopathy, childhood disability, maternal side effects (e.g., nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), maternal antibiotic use, maternal satisfaction, neonatal infection, and neonatal antibiotic use, were not reported in the included trials. In conclusion, the review found no evidence that high-dose oxytocin increases the likelihood of vaginal delivery within 24 hours or reduces the cesarean section rate. While high-dose regimens may shorten the induction-to-delivery interval, this finding is limited by the quality of the included studies. High-dose oxytocin was associated with an increased risk of uterine hyperstimulation, but the clinical implications of this finding remain unclear. Further high-quality trials are needed to evaluate the effects of high-dose oxytocin regimens on a comprehensive range of maternal and neonatal outcomes.
